By the end, Doug is a pencil-sized white alligator,

Decades.
The White Gorilla.
His name was Snowflake, and he fathered twenty-two babies at Barcelona Zoo
without a single one of them coming out white.
He was born wild in Equatorial Guinea and brought to the zoo as a baby in nineteen sixty-six.
He was an albino, which means his body made almost no melanin,
the dark pigment that colours skin, hair and eyes and also shields skin from the sun.
His eyes were pale blue, his vision was weak, and bright light bothered him.
Here's the strange part.
In twenty thirteen, scientists read Snowflake's genome and traced his albinism to a single changed letter in one pigment gene, which he carried twice.
They checked about two point six billion letters of his genome.
Reading that many aloud at one letter a second would take more than eighty years,
twice as long as Snowflake lived.
The genome also suggests his parents were close relatives,
most likely an uncle and his niece, the first inbreeding ever reported in a wild-born gorilla of his kind.
The rarest gorilla on Earth was a family accident.
The five babies who were tested each carried only one copy of the changed letter,
and one copy is not enough to turn a gorilla white.
To keep Snowflake's memory alive, Doug is sitting in full sun all afternoon in a white gorilla suit.
Doug did not agree to this.
The suit has no melanin either.
Doug has died. Again.
Snowflake had a zoo and forty years,
but out in the open, white gets far less time, except in one ocean.
The White Whale.
An all-white humpback called Migaloo was first seen off Byron Bay, Australia, in nineteen ninety-one,
and he was still being reported off the coast in twenty twenty.
A skin sample showed that he is male,
and a later gene study found both copies of a key pigment gene broken, which points to a true albino.
In twenty twenty-two, a dead white humpback washed up in Victoria,
but tests showed it was a female, so it wasn't him.
So why is he still around? The catch is who hunts humpbacks.
When mammal-eating orcas go after humpbacks, they target the calves,
so a fully grown humpback has almost nothing left to hide from.
Queensland even declared him a special interest whale,
so boats must stay at least five hundred meters away from him, and aircraft six hundred and ten.
That status is only for whales that are totally white or more than ninety percent white.
Five hundred meters is about five football pitches of empty water around one whale.
Doug, in a small white whale costume, has drifted well inside the zone,
and the only thing that comes for him is a ranger with a megaphone.
Doug is fine.
The narrator had something bigger in mind.
A white animal lasts decades only where nothing big enough is hunting it,
and on land, something always is.
The White Lion.
The white lions of Timbavati in South Africa look like the most doomed animals on the savanna,
and they are not even albino.
They are leucistic, the second kind of white animal.
A recessive change in a pigment gene whitens the coat,
but the eyes keep their colour, usually golden or blue-grey, and they work normally.
Remember that difference, because it matters for what comes next.
On dry grass, a white lion stands out like a sheet of printer paper dropped on a brown carpet.
You would expect them to starve,
but a study of white lions released into a fenced reserve found that they hunted about as well as the tawny lions living there.
But that's not the disturbing part.
The disturbing part is what it means for the true albinos.
Albino mammals are born with retinas that don't develop properly,
and some nerve fibres from each eye cross to the wrong side of the brain.
The coat alone doesn't stop a lion hunting. The eyes are what make it worse.
Most of the true albinos from here on have both problems,
a coat that gives them away and eyes that can't see what's coming.
Doug has walked across the savanna to tell a white lioness how nice her coat is.
"hi friend?"
Her eyes work perfectly, and she saw him long before he said it.
Doug has died. Again.
From here on, every white animal that lasts more than a season has a fence, a law or a zoo around it.
Years.
The White Deer.
The biggest herd of white deer in the world only exists because the army fenced it in by accident.
In nineteen forty-one, the army built the Seneca Army Depot in New York
and ran a fence about thirty-nine kilometers long around it, almost the length of a marathon.
A herd of white-tailed deer was trapped inside.
Some of the deer born behind that fence were white,
and they are leucistic, with white coats and normal brown eyes that see perfectly well.
In the nineteen fifties, the depot's commander ordered that the white deer be protected,
and the white part of the herd grew to roughly two hundred animals.
Being shut in for decades has also left the herd heavily inbred.
True albino deer are far rarer,
about one deer in thirty thousand by the Missouri Department of Conservation's estimate,
and they often have poor eyesight that makes surviving in the wild difficult.
Here's the problem.
The fence that trapped the deer also kept the coyotes out,
and a conservationist working to protect the herd has said these deer wouldn't last more than a season in the wild.
Even with good eyes, white survives behind a fence.
Doug has stepped outside the fence for a stretch.
Nothing out here wants a stick man.
It wants the white one, which is why Doug is the white one.
Doug has died. Again.
The deer gets a fence,
and the next one gets an entire town council.
The White Squirrel.
In one Illinois town, harassing a white squirrel can cost you a seven hundred and fifty dollar fine.
The town is Olney, and its white squirrels are true albinos,
which by local law have right of way on every public street and sidewalk in town.
In practice, the town mostly enforces the fine when someone hits one with a car on purpose.
A whole town wrote laws for an animal that weighs about as much as a bottle of water.
Every October, volunteers spend three days counting them,
a tradition that started in nineteen seventy-seven.
Reports from nineteen forty-one described about eight hundred albino squirrels in Olney,
and the twenty twenty-four count found eighty-one, up from seventy-three the year before.
The worst part is the eyes.
With no pigment in them, glare from the sun can blind an albino squirrel for a moment,
which makes it much harder to spot what's coming.
What's coming is usually a cat.
Free-roaming cats are the squirrels' main predator,
so in two thousand two, the town banned cats from roaming free.
Doug, in a white squirrel costume, is crossing Main Street, and every car in town has stopped for him.
This cat is not roaming free.
Its lead is just very long.
Doug has died. Again.
The squirrel gets lawyers, but the next one only gets its feathers, and they're wearing out.
The White Bird.
An albino bird's feathers wear out faster than a normal bird's,
because the pigment it's missing is also what makes feathers tough.
One study tested feather keratin and found the dark kind was harder,
so pale keratin would need to be about forty percent thicker to stand up to the same wear.
Picture white sneakers worn every day on gravel,
except the sneakers are how you escape.
In a British survey of birds with unusual plumage, over three-quarters were classed as leucistic, with dark eyes that work.
Some white birds with reddish eyes have a different condition that keeps a little working pigment,
and they see much better than albinos do.
The British Trust for Ornithology, which ran the survey, says that seeing an adult albino in the wild is very unlikely,
because its bad eyesight means its survival prospects are poor.
The cruel part is that an albino bird is losing on two fronts at once.
It can't see the hawk coming,
and when it finally flees, the wings carrying it are wearing out underneath it.
Nothing out here wanted a stick man, which is why Doug is a bird,
flapping hard and losing a feather with every stroke.
Doug has died. Again.
A bird at least gets to fly before it fails,
but the next one has to crawl, alone, in the dark.
Day one.
The White Turtle.
In twenty sixteen, an albino green turtle hatchling on Castaways Beach in Queensland
stayed in its nest for two days after its brothers and sisters had already left.
A volunteer who found it said it wasn't sick, it was just white.
This one started its life two days behind.
Sea turtle hatchlings usually come out at night, partly to avoid the predators that hunt by day,
and a typical green turtle nest holds between one hundred and two hundred eggs.
On the short run to the water, crabs and gulls pick them off,
and once they reach the sea, fish take their share.
About one hatchling in a thousand is estimated to reach adulthood.
That's eighty-three egg cartons full of babies for one grown turtle.
This is the part that matters.
Hatchlings survive the run on numbers, because the crabs and the gulls can't catch all of them at once.
This one ran with no crowd at all.
It ran alone, and it was white.
It did reach the sea, and that volunteer said it took off into the water as happy as can be.
That's where the record ends.
Doug, in a white turtle costume, is two days late and crossing the beach by himself, very slowly, under a full moon.
Every crab on the beach turns around.
Doug has died.
The turtle had the sea a few meters away,
but the last one hatches in a swamp, and the swamp is full of birds.
The White Alligator.
According to the South Carolina Aquarium, most albino alligators born in the wild
don't survive more than about twenty-four hours.
A newly hatched alligator is about twenty-one to twenty-three centimeters long, a little longer than a new pencil.
Florida's wildlife agency says small alligators are eaten by raccoons, otters, wading birds and fish,
and that bigger alligators may be the worst threat of all.
A dark hatchling disappears into dark water,
but a white one is the brightest thing in the swamp.
One co-founder of a Florida park that breeds them compared it to Skittles.
Its skin burns easily,
and the aquarium says its eyes are so sensitive to bright light that its vision is impaired.
And this is the real twist.
A grown alligator is one of the toughest animals alive,
but an albino one almost never gets to grow up outside a zoo.
Claude, one of fewer than two hundred albino alligators thought to exist,
hatched on a Louisiana farm in nineteen ninety-five
and lived to thirty at a San Francisco museum, in shade, behind glass.
